subject: biology

moments.title: Hooke sees cells in cork
moments.body:
Hooke, working with a primitive microscope, looks at a slice of cork. He sees small empty chambers — 'cells', he says, because they remind him of monks' rooms. He publishes the observation in Micrographia (1665), one of the first illustrated scientific books.

The cells he sees are dead — just the walls of plant cells. He doesn't see the contents, doesn't understand the structure, and doesn't generalise to other organisms.
moments.takeaway: The word 'cell' enters biology. The biological significance takes nearly two centuries to emerge.

moments.title: Van Leeuwenhoek's 'animalcules'
moments.body:
A self-taught microscope maker, van Leeuwenhoek produces single-lens microscopes magnifying up to 270x — far better than Hooke's. He sees moving creatures in pond water, dental plaque, vinegar. He calls them 'animalcules'.

The Royal Society in London is skeptical until they send observers. Van Leeuwenhoek is the first person to see bacteria.
moments.takeaway: A whole microbial world is visible — but no one knows what to make of it for another two centuries.

moments.title: Schleiden and Schwann formalise cell theory
moments.who: Matthias Schleiden (botanist) and Theodor Schwann (zoologist), Berlin
moments.body:
Schleiden proposes that all plant tissues are composed of cells (1838). Schwann generalises to animals (1839), proposing that all living organisms are made of cells.

They are right but their mechanism (free-cell formation, like crystallisation) is wrong. Cells, they thought, formed by aggregation of formless material.
moments.takeaway: All life is cellular. The unifying principle of modern biology is in place.

moments.title: Virchow — omnis cellula e cellula
moments.body:
Virchow corrects Schleiden and Schwann: cells do not form spontaneously, they come from pre-existing cells. 'Omnis cellula e cellula' — every cell from a cell.

This closes the loop: cells are the units of life, and they reproduce. Combined with germ theory, this overturns spontaneous generation at every scale.

quote.text: Where a cell exists, there must have been a preexisting cell.

moments.takeaway: Cells come from cells. Biology has its first universal generalisation about how life perpetuates.

now.title: Cells today
now.body:
Cell biology is a discipline of its own. Fluorescence microscopy (Nobel 2014 for super-resolution: Betzig, Hell, Moerner) lets us see structures at 20-nanometre resolution. Live-cell imaging tracks single molecules. Single-cell sequencing reveals heterogeneity within tissues.

We understand cells as integrated systems: organelles, cytoskeleton, signaling networks. Synthetic biology engineers cells for purpose-built functions.
now.open_questions: How did the first cell originate? What's the minimal set of genes for a free-living cell (Venter's lab made one with 473 genes in 2016)? Can we build a cell from scratch (bottom-up)? Why do some unicellular organisms become multicellular?

reflection: Hooke's word 'cell' was a casual descriptive choice — based on how the cork looked. Two centuries later it had become the most fundamental concept in biology. How much does scientific language shape the development of theory, and how much does theory force a re-evaluation of language?
